claims.claim_text: Almost every serial link in practice uses the same framing — eight data bits, no parity, one stop bit — so the only settings a user has to get right are the baud rate and which port to open.
claims.quote_verbatim: eight bits, no parody, one stop bit
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Only A Transmitter

claims.claim_text: The two ends must share a ground reference; without it the transmit and receive lines carry nothing regardless of what the firmware is doing.
claims.quote_verbatim: RX and TX won't transmit if there's no ground linking them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Swapping transmit and receive is the standard error, and swapping it twice on the same board cancels out, which is how a link sometimes works by accident.
claims.quote_verbatim: I actually swapped RX and TX twice on the board by accident
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: When nothing comes back, the first move is to put an oscilloscope or other external instrument on the line and establish whether anything is being transmitted at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: stick a scope or something else external on there just to see if it's pumping anything out
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Only A Transmitter

claims.claim_text: A protocol analyser is not self-explanatory: it decodes correctly only if it is set up correctly — the software timeout on an SPI capture, for instance — so it supplements knowing the protocol rather than replacing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to set your software time out right. Otherwise it doesn't decode your data properly
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Only A Transmitter

claims.claim_text: Not every periodic signal on the expected pin is the expected signal: a waveform taken for serial output turned out to change its packet length as a hand approached the board, which identified it as something other than the UART.
claims.quote_verbatim: this data packet is actually changing length as my hand gets closer to it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PITA Package

claims.claim_text: Writing a transmitter and a receiver is the standard first exercise in a serial protocols course, with an LED toggled on receipt of a known character so the student can see it working before anything else is attempted.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone in my training ends up writing a UART transmitter and receiver on day one
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: Hardware serial is now assumed on any microcontroller alongside SPI and I2C, but it was not always: the cheapest parts had no serial peripheral at all, and designers bit-banged their own on general-purpose pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've had to bit bang my own UARTs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mars, System Design & NAND - Mercurial Mars Mission

claims.claim_text: One major vendor was slow to put serial peripherals into its low-end parts, which is why designers moved to competing families that had one or two, and the gap persisted for years before it was closed.
claims.quote_verbatim: microchip took quite a while before they started putting UARTs in their lowest end devices
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: At the very bottom of the market the peripheral still does not exist: a three-cent microcontroller has no hardware serial, so its output is bit-banged in software on an ordinary I/O pin.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't have a hardware UART in it for three cents
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PITA Package

claims.claim_text: Peripherals can be wrong in silicon rather than in firmware: on one part the two serial ports were transposed — the pins as well as the registers — and the fact was added to the errata sheet months after release, after users had spent time debugging a port that could not work.
claims.quote_verbatim: serial port one is actually serial port two of Weisford
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Some microcontrollers carry an internal routing matrix, comparable to the routing inside an FPGA, so a serial peripheral can be assigned to almost any pin rather than to a fixed pair.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have an internal routing logic, kind of like, you know, an analog FPGA routing thing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: That flexibility is not usually a reason to choose a part, but it rescues layouts: it removes the situation in which the required peripheral is on a pin that cannot be escaped.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's probably not a reason to design it in
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Tiny Lab Movement

claims.claim_text: The board designer and the firmware engineer pull in opposite directions over which serial pins to use, because the convenient pin to escape from a ball grid array is rarely the default peripheral pin. Deliberately using a different instance on a second board is a good way to learn where the configuration actually lives.
claims.quote_verbatim: force yourself to use a different UART because, like, man, that's such a great way to learn
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson
claims.episode_title: Embedded Linux with Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: Flexible peripheral blocks are allocated, not free: where a device offers four instances that can each be configured as SPI, I2C or serial, using all four as serial ports leaves nothing for the other two protocols.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could have up to four UARTs, but if you have four UARTs, that means you can't have any I squared C or any spy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pseudo Code...Pseudo Good

claims.claim_text: On a Linux single-board computer the pin has to be in serial mode before anything works: if the board table does not already list it as a serial port, a configuration tool must switch that pin's peripheral function.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to use the config pin tool to change that peripheral to a UART
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Once the pin is in the right mode the port is reached through the device node and any ordinary serial library will do, whatever the language.
claims.quote_verbatim: just talk to it through dev TTY
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: The same pin can be switched between functions at run time — put into serial mode to talk to one device, then back to SPI to talk to another — which is possible and rarely advisable.
claims.quote_verbatim: Put it in UART mode. Talk to the UART device. Put it back to spy mode.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Moving the console from one serial instance to another on an embedded Linux system was not a configuration change: register values had to be found and changed in about ten separate places in the kernel source tree, and the exercise took over a month for someone new to it.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like 10 different places in the kernel source tree that I had to go find and change these register values
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Adding a second serial port breaks the habitual output path: the standard print function targets one port, so a second requires a function that takes the port as an argument or otherwise selects between them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to like write a new function basically that switch allows you to switch between the two
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Optimization Beast

claims.claim_text: A well-implemented peripheral will run at baud rates up to a quarter of the peripheral clock, which puts 12 megabaud within reach on a conventional microcontroller — a rate at which a receive FIFO stops being optional.
claims.quote_verbatim: it will do board rates up to a quarter of the clock rate
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Meracious Mike Manuduction

claims.claim_text: The defect to check for in a FIFO implementation is a missing timeout interrupt: if the interrupt only fires at a fill threshold, a burst that ends short of it sits in the FIFO indefinitely, which shows up as the last few bytes of a large transfer never arriving. The workaround is a timer interrupt set a few microseconds after the last byte that drains whatever remains.
claims.quote_verbatim: What is usually the problem is getting the last few bytes out of a big transfer
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Meracious Mike Manuduction

claims.claim_text: Reusing an open-source core is not automatically cheaper than writing one: a core emulating a full 16C550 with multiple baud rates and framing options occupied more area than the CPU next to it, where the actual requirement — 9600 baud in each direction — fits in twenty or thirty flip-flops written directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: this core was actually taking up more space than the CPU was
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Cores from public repositories vary widely in quality and are often aimed at a different problem, so the practical filters are who wrote it and how recently it was updated.
claims.quote_verbatim: it helps to like look at the author's name
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Hardening a serial port into an FPGA is a poor use of silicon: it is a small block of logic running slowly, and the vendor cannot predict how many a given customer wants or which features they need.
claims.quote_verbatim: Putting a UART onto an FPGA, dumbest idea in the book
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Demand for serial ports on small boards exceeds what the parts provide, which is why bit-banging libraries exist for something as basic as a serial port; software serial on a small board tops out around 9600 baud and is not always reliable, particularly when it is also carrying debug output.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're using software serial, depending on the board you're running on, you're only going to get 9,600 or a little bit more baud
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: The soft system-on-chip inverts the selection problem: instead of hunting for a microcontroller with exactly the right number of serial ports, an existing core is taken and the one missing peripheral is added, which turns firmware that would have relied on DMA tricks and bit-banging into something simple.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of looking for a microcontroller that has just the right number of UARTs
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains at 35c3

claims.claim_text: The extreme cases make the argument plainly: a controller needing thirty-two serial outputs from one unit is far easier to build by driving data into an FPGA and splitting it than by finding a microcontroller with thirty-two ports.
claims.quote_verbatim: try finding a microcontroller that has 32 UARTs in it
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains at 35c3

claims.claim_text: The same requirement is one of the standing arguments for custom silicon: a part with sixteen serial ports is hard to buy off the shelf but straightforward to specify if the chip is being made.
claims.quote_verbatim: it would be really hard to buy a off the shelf microcontroller that had 16 UARTs
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Where soft cores are used at scale, a small number of well-supported blocks become de facto standards even for something as simple as a serial port, so the same peripheral appears regardless of which processor is chosen — though the software still talks to it through a driver rather than by writing registers directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might end up using the same UART that everybody else is using because it's really well supported
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: A programmable I/O block takes a third position between hardware and bit-banging: small stripped-down processors that are very good at deterministic high-speed bit-banging and poor at everything else. The timing-critical part of a software peripheral is pushed onto them and then accessed through FIFOs and DMA as if it were a hardware block, so the resource can be committed to extra serial ports — or to protocols nobody would commit to silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: you take the timing sensitive part of a software peripheral. You push that onto the PIO cores, you offload it
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: That last case is the distinctive one: an addressable LED protocol was driven with zero processor overhead by feeding a state machine over DMA, which is not something a chip vendor would build a dedicated peripheral for.
claims.quote_verbatim: which we can do with zero overhead just by DMAing into a PIO state machine
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A peripheral can be repurposed when the one needed is absent: a codec requiring I2S on a part with no I2S support was driven by pressing the serial peripheral into service for the I2S bus and bit-banging the remaining pins, with about eight instructions of timing margin to work in.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had to connect the I2C, um, UART to the I2, um, the I2S bus and do a couple of bit banging
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: Serial input is a good argument for interrupts over polling: an interrupt from the peripheral can deliver a meaningful block of data and then signal a task to wake, rather than a task spending cycles checking at some interval. Systems built that way scale better, respond faster and use less power, since an event-driven design lets the processor stay asleep.
claims.quote_verbatim: your UART peripheral has, or, you know, USART spy, whatever, whatever it is, right? Some sort of serial peripheral has interrupts
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: A reliable sign that a long-running computation should become its own task is finding oneself adding a check on the serial port every hundred iterations of a loop to avoid a buffer overflow and dropped characters.
claims.quote_verbatim: every hundred iterations of this loop, I should, I need to go check on the UART to make sure that I don't get, you know, a buffer overflow
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: A serial console is a useful skeleton to start a project from: it needs the serial peripheral, and once it exists the other drivers can each be exercised from it, so the system is built up from working pieces rather than from a blank page.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I start with a serial console and that means I need a UR
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pedantic or Andrantic

claims.claim_text: The case for including a shell over the serial port in an embedded project is not obvious until testing is considered, at which point it becomes the thing that unlocks automation; lightweight shell implementations are widely available.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lightweight shell, you can find any number of examples online on how to like build a lightweight shell over you are
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: Describing hardware separately from code is what makes a board change cheap: a device tree records that a serial port exists at a given address in a particular chip's memory map, and swapping a sensor or a board becomes a different overlay file rather than a change to the C.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have a UART, the UART is at this address in the memory map of this specific chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: That uniform description is machine-readable at ecosystem scale: with hundreds of platforms all describing which chip has how many serial ports and where they sit on the bus, simulation configurations can be generated automatically for all of them rather than written by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: which chip has how many UARTs and so on. All of this information we're getting from Zephyr
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: From the software's point of view one serial peripheral is much like another — the registers and memory map differ but the behaviour does not — which is the argument for choosing hardware by what the application needs rather than mapping the application onto whatever was available.
claims.quote_verbatim: whether it's this UART or that UART, like it's just literally a difference of the registers are different
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A simulator can stand in for the board during development: the binary runs, the console output appears, and an interactive terminal is available, along with a log of every peripheral access.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're going to get UART output in Windows
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Simulating Embedded Hardware with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: An initialised but unused serial block is a real power cost: one design was drawing over 200 microamps through a peripheral that was not being used, recovered by de-initialising the block and removing its power.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you are not using UART, you are consuming, you know, 200, more than 200 microampere
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal
claims.episode_title: Blogging Electronics with Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: Payload size on the link is a power decision too: replacing a 200-byte JSON packet with a 16-byte encoding cut hundreds of microamps from the same product.
claims.quote_verbatim: one company was sending 200 bytes to mobile phone using JSON packet
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal
claims.episode_title: Blogging Electronics with Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: Clock gating and power gating are not the same option: the clock to a serial peripheral can be disabled to save dynamic power, but the block cannot be individually powered down, because defining a separate power region per peripheral costs placement density that would otherwise hold logic.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can disable the clock to a UR and that saves you some dynamic power. You cannot individually power down the UR.
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Coarser power modes exist around the peripheral: a mode that stops the clocks to everything except the serial port, and a dormant mode that stops all clocks until a pin changes, from which software resumes exactly where it stopped as though no time had passed.
claims.quote_verbatim: I only need to use the UART. So turn off the clocks to everything apart from the UART
claims.speaker: Liam Fraser
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A 115,200 baud link is a small pipe, and forcing both operational data and debug data through it means one has to be sacrificed, usually the debugging.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have a, you aren't running at like 115 K, then like you could only get so much data through that
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: The design response is not to widen the debug channel but to remove the distinction: rather than attaching JTAG and dumping data over serial during bring-up — acceptable for a product that will end up in a case on a shelf — work out how to carry that information in the data stream the system already produces, because a launch vehicle cannot be probed in flight.
claims.quote_verbatim: figure out how you can get that data in the sort of data stream that you're already consuming
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Input validation on a serial stream can create the fault it was meant to prevent: a driver that discarded any byte above 127 as line noise crashed deployed units in one country, because the cell tower name being reported contained an accented character encoded above that threshold.
claims.quote_verbatim: if the, the character of the byte was zero or greater than 127, they're like, oh, this must be UART noise
claims.speaker: Alvaro Prieto
claims.episode_title: Reunion Impedance Matching and 2023 Predictions

claims.claim_text: A module carrying the whole protocol stack on board removes a porting problem: a small microcontroller with tens of kilobytes of flash cannot host a Bluetooth host stack, so a module that exposes the finished service over a serial link and takes data in and out is what makes the design possible at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can just communicate directly over UART, for example.
claims.speaker: Jeff Roberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: The same pattern applies to adding connectivity generally: a second chip is placed alongside the main processor and spoken to over a serial link, which keeps the main firmware small and the vendor's stack at arm's length.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to put an ESP8266 as a secondary chip. And then, you know, use a UART to talk to it.
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Serial is also the production test interface: a jig at the end of the line sends a command, takes a measurement, sends another and takes another, producing a per-unit test report alongside programming and voltage checks.
claims.quote_verbatim: sending a command, taking a measurement, send another command, take a measurement
claims.speaker: Pete Staples
claims.episode_title: Standardizing Manufacturing with Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: The boot console is the standard entry point for examining a device that was not meant to be examined: connecting to a couple of pins and reading what the bootloader prints establishes what the system is.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's pretty basic stuff, hooking up a UART to a couple of pins
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: That entry point has been closing: over about five years vendors stopped marking JTAG and serial test points, disabled the consoles and disabled JTAG. The longer-term trajectory is a board with one or two pieces of silicon and no test points at all, where anything short of an attack on the silicon becomes very difficult.
claims.quote_verbatim: suddenly vendors have stopped obviously marking JTAG and UART test points
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe FitzPatrick

claims.claim_text: Debug access on a finished product is a physical operation: wires soldered to the JTAG header and to the serial pins, which break, leaving the engineer unsure whether they are debugging their code or their soldering.
claims.quote_verbatim: You need to like solder wires so you can access, you know, your JTAG header and you need to, you know, find out where your UART pins are
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: A phone can serve as the console: a terminal application with a serial option, connected to the board over USB, gives an interactive shell for reading sensor output and issuing commands without a laptop, provided the target supports serial over its USB connection.
claims.quote_verbatim: I plugged in a Zephyr board that had a UART on it. And I plugged it into my phone, USB-C to USB-C.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: Instrument automation converges on the same interface: a parser that consumes serial output can drive any instrument whose interface ultimately resolves to a serial port, whatever the physical connection.
claims.quote_verbatim: anything that has, that anything ultimately resolves, you can do Bluetooth meters and other instruments, but only if they resolve down to a UART serial port
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Voltage, Vibes, and VOCs

claims.claim_text: The dedicated serial interface chip is one of the components conventionally listed as having changed the industry, alongside the first flash-programmable microcontroller and the first ARM processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: Everyone takes UARTs for granted
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

name: UART
